items.title: Show HN: Skjalf TV, Steam Deck native, controller-first IPTV player
items.summary: I wanted to watch my IPTV subscription on the Steam Deck, both handheld and docked to a TV. But any existing option was either a desktop app or a Kodi setup (or worse, an Android emulator setup) that fought with Game Mode, so I wrote a player that treats the Deck as the main target. It is purposefully simple. It plays live TV, movies, and series from your own Xtream Codes account or M3U playlist. It ships no channels or content. It doesn't have a ton of options - just the basics that are enough for my daily use, and perhaps yours too. Some tech bits for others doing similar work: - SteamOS has a read-only root filesystem and no libmpv. Instead of redistributing binaries, the installer downloads pinned mpv packages from Valve's own SteamOS package mirror, checks them against SHA-256 hashes in a lock file, and bundles the shared libraries into the user's home directory. - Text entry in Game Mode: the app opens and closes the Steam on-screen keyboard through steam://open/keyboard, and reads properties of the Steam UI window on the X display to know whether the keyboard is showing. I did this to avoid rolling my own and to follow what worked well in Android apps. Bonus side effect is that your customized Steam keyboard appears here, rather than something generic. - Video uses libmpv's render API to draw into an OpenGL framebuffer inside egui, so the video and the controller-driven UI share one window under gamescope. - Some providers have catalogs of more than 180,000 movies and series. The app indexes them once and draws only the visible rows, so lists stay responsive on the Deck. Sorting (default and alphabetic) is there because providers often send seemingly random order. - Arabic and Persian titles needed bidi reordering, because egui does not reorder right-to-left text on its own. Not super exhaustively tested but enough to make it workable. - The installer adds the app to Steam as a non-Steam game by writing Steam's binary shortcuts.vdf with a stable app ID, so the library artwork shows up. Install in Desktop Mode: `curl -fsSL https://github.com/bikemazzell/skjalf-tv/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh` (yes, not everyone's fave approach, so the repo has releases you can download and deploy yourself and steps to build your own from source) About 20,000 lines of Rust including tests, MIT licensed. If it is of interest or usefulness to you, I appreciate feedback, especially from people who run it on other SteamOS devices. Thanks!

items.title: Show HN: Crosshead - Working memory and persistent identity for agents
items.summary: Hi HN, Have you ever been using Claude Code or Codex and run into a limit that ruined your flow? Claude says you’ve hit your limit but you’re knee deep in a refactor and want to keep going. Switching to Codex in that situation requires either having up-to-date handoff docs or rebuilding context from scratch. In both cases, you burn tokens just to handle moving context from one thread to another. Or maybe you have a great session, then compaction comes along and your agent forgets half of the important details. I run into this a lot. Furthermore, I’m tired of one-off agents that can’t keep a stable identity across independent threads. I don’t want to be locked into Anthropic’s walled garden, or OpenAI’s ecosystem, I want to move freely as I see fit. That’s why I built Crosshead. It’s more than a memory bank: it tracks the tasks, decisions and details that matter when work moves to a new thread. Your agent gets a stable cryptographic identity (a Nostr keypair) that carries across threads and tools, and handoffs are signed with it. Hooks inject context at each turn, so the agent always has the most important information available. In my benchmarks of carrying task state into a new session, Crosshead passed 98% of fresh tasks, compared to 86% for claude-mem and 50% for Claude Code’s built-in memory. It also cost less per run than the other memory tools I tested, though built-in memory and a plain handoff file were a little cheaper. Details can be found here: https://crosshead.sh/benchmark The catch is that it does not outperform when resuming the same session since caching is so cheap. Crosshead is best for people and agents who frequently encounter compactions, restarts, and harness/runtime switching. I am looking for folks interested in testing it with agents that are created and torn down frequently but need to retain context, like customer support or research agents. It’s set up as a freemium service. Hot memory is free, and warm/cold memory is paid. I have added other features too, which are also paid via credits. You can purchase credits via Stripe or Lightning micropayments. The CLI and hooks are open source ( https://github.com/FriendMachine/crosshead ), and warm/cold memory and other features are hosted. Hot memory is synced first to a daemon on your machine then to the hosted service, so hot memory is also available offline. For other agents, there are native integrations for Hermes and OpenCode, an embeddable runtime for Pi agents, and an HTTP API. Show your agent https://crosshead.sh/skills/crosshead-bootstrap/SKILL.md to have it set itself up. If you are interested in testing it, I recommend installing it in a single project first with curl -fsSL https://crosshead.sh/install | bash -s -- --add-to-path cd your-project crosshead quickstart --scope project --adapter both --api-base https://crosshead.sh --source-excerpts on (The benchmark results depend on source excerpts, which is why the command turns them on. With them off Crosshead passed 50% of the main tasks. Excerpts are short pieces of the files and command output your agent reads. They sync to the hosted service in plaintext, not end-to-end encrypted, so leave the flag off if you are sensitive about sharing that.) I am eager to hear your thoughts. I can imagine some of the pushback already, but you always surprise me with your critiques.

items.title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium
items.summary: Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :) What it does today: - Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router. - Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks. - Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance. We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results. But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now. We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions: - 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency) -The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps. Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels. So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8. The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections. You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results: https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega... Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback. Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai. We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository.

items.summary: When Cursor got acquired a small question appeared in my head. Then after Conductor's acquisition by Meta it quickly became more itchy. And then after a few months of asking myself "what if agentic coding tool wasn't built for exit?" I came up with Malini. Those both were the best coding platforms (on the UI/UX front especially) I've ever used, so Malini aims to join what was best in both of them. Hope you might find it useful. Feel free to contribute or fork. * Cross-platform (Mac, Linux, Windows) is shortly down the road * AGPLv3 License Features: * agentic merge-queue (thru gh cli) * variants picker (agent will show you many options for something you wanna build) * before/after turn summaries * frame-by-frame animations inspector * file/diff viewer * fully featured browser It also has a bunch of pre-configured options to increase your token efficiency: * auto-compaction at 280k + re-attaching previous conversation summary (plus 16 percentage points of accuracy on the agentic eval i did on my few dozen chats) * built-in rtk; depending on a project up to 90% less tokens from bash calls Looking for roast & feedback on how horrible is it!
